title: Adaptability
snippet:
Adaptability -  Dark Souls II - mechanic - agility 
 agility : Increased by both Adaptability and Attunement, where Adaptability is more beneficial. ADP levels Agility three times faster than Attunement.
Hard-capped at 120 with both Adaptability and Attunement at 99.
Improves Estus consumption animation. The item consume speed multiplier only changes between 90 and 100 Agility. At the lowest possible Agility your Estus consume speed is 2.5 seconds, at 100 Agility it takes just over 2 second to complete the Estus consumption animation.
Improves Weapon swap speed. This multiplier scales from 120% at minimum Agility up to 145% at maximum Agility.
Improves speed of guard raise animation. This multiplier scales from 100% at minimum Agility up to 150% at maximum Agility.
Additional invincibility frames while rolling and backstepping - see charts below.

title: Adaptability
snippet:
Compared to Dark Souls, 96 Agility will give you 11 i-frames which is the same as all roll types except for Dark Wood Gain Ring roll type which is 13 iframes.

Rolling with insufficient stamina will cause iFrames to be reduced on those rolls.

title: Adaptability
snippet:
Adaptability -  Dark Souls II - mechanic - dark_souls_2_iframe_charts 
 dark_souls_2_iframe_charts : "Investment" tiers exist to compensate for the overlapping menu display values of Agility in different tiers. For example 110 AGL is the menu display for 7 internal values, the subindexes on AGL numbers accomplish the same function (x).

"Investment" = ADP x .75 + ATN x .25 rounded down to the nearest whole number. ADP levels Agility three times faster than Attunement does.

The Agility displayed in your player status screen might not always accurately reflect the in-game math and iFrames the player character has. As an example, when Agility is calculated to be less than 85 it will be set to a value of 85 regardless. When players start the game before picking a class and character name, they will be at soul level negative 44, but Agility will still be displayed as 85. This correlates on the chart with tier 1 investment 85(a) AGL.

title: Adaptability
snippet: There are several more points where the menu display will remain at the same display value but iFrames are gained between them, such as the displayed value of 110 which can be 13 or 14 iFrames on rolls, or the display value of 112 which can be 8 or 9 iFrames on backsteps. Agility investment was made to describe these true iFrame values since they are not displayed in a meaningful way by the game. The above chart only shows points at which the player character gains iFrames, to see the raw data for all AGL investment visit [https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/18JuYshFKmHm2wkyUmxnBV6B34799QdbBpuHVG6IMrHM/edit?gid=1780049913#gid=1780049913 this spreadsheet].

title: Adaptability
snippet: Bandit, Warrior and Cleric class all have 85 Agility displayed in the menu, though Bandit class has a lower amount of iFrames. Bandit class starts with 2 Attunement and 3 Adaptability which calculates to Agility investment tier 2 giving 7 iframes on rolls, this is reflected on the above chart as 85(b) Agility. Warrior and Cleric class are calculated to tier 5 investment 85(e) which is 8 iFrames on rolls, though all three classes have in menu values of 85 Agility. This means that when starting as Bandit players will need to invest more points to get to 86 agility compared with these other classes that start with higher Adaptability and Attunement. It is important to note that the crucial breakpoints of 92, 96 and 99 Agility will always accurately match with the menu display, In addition, the less important breakpoints of 88 and 105 will also match menu values when calculating your agility investment tier.

title: Adaptability
snippet:
Adaptability -  Dark Souls II - mechanic - invincibility_frames_iframes 
 invincibility_frames_iframes : Invincibility frames (or i-frames) are the frames during rolls that a character are invincible to enemies' attacks, measured in 1/30ths of a second (or about 0.0333... seconds each).

Invincibility frames are increased in a non-linear way, affected by Agility rather than Equip Load, with Equip Load only affecting distance when rolling.

Agility has specific breakpoints in which you gain iFrames, they are the stopping points you will want to meet as you level. The only breakpoints worth caring about are **92/96/99 Agility**, these are important because you do not gain additional rolling iframes between breakpoints. This means that having 95 Agility is the same as having 92 Agility in terms of iframes.

Compared to Dark Souls, 96 Agility will give you 11 i-frames which is the same as all roll types except for Dark Wood Gain Ring roll type which is 13 iframes.

title: Adaptability
snippet:
Adaptability -  Dark Souls II - mechanic - general_information 
 general_information : Adaptability is the combination of Resistance and an Agility stat (from the beta tests). Raising Adaptability increases Poise and more importantly raises the substat called Agility.

Improving Adaptability also raises all status defenses (i.e. Poison, Bleed, Curse and Petrify), whilst also raising the player's HP and Poison Attack Bonus slightly. Finally, Adaptability is also complementary with the Endurance stat, in that raising the two stats at the same rate will grant extra natural Poise.

title: Bandit (Dark Souls II)
snippet:
Bandit (Dark Souls II) -  Dark Souls II - mechanic - lead 
 lead : The **Bandit** is one of the classes in *Dark Souls 2*.

It has high Dexterity and well above average Faith, meaning it lends itself rather well towards builds focused either on both or only the former (though it will have strong competition from the Swordsman when it comes to pure Dexterity builds). It is rather unsuitable to spells, even the Miracle ones, due to its extremely low Attunement and Intelligence.

Bandits are actually unable to speak to Straid of Olaphis by default, the only class that can't do that, due to its extremely low Intelligence not meeting his minimum required amount of 3.

title: Bandit (Dark Souls II)
snippet: There is a curious disadvantage to its high Vitality, higher than any other starting class: when using the Third Dragon Ring, it cannot receive the full benefit of the Flynn's Ring and will get a light decrease of 4 Attack Rating compared to any other class.

title: Bandit (Dark Souls II)
snippet:
Until an unlimited source of arrows is acquired, they are best either saved for trying to pull individual enemies from groups or ambushes, or for trying to kill one of the early Ogres (either the one outside the Firekeeper's Hut in Things Betwixt at the start of the tutorial that also holds the Stone Ring, or the Scholar of the First Sin-exclusive one on the way towards the Forest of Fallen Giants) for a large amount of extra Souls.

The class's Bandit Set is actually fairly good, as it has somewhat high physical defences and is, together with the Knight's partial Falconer Set, the only starting set with decent starting Poise.

Due to its very low Adaptability and Attunement it has a substandard roll (only 7 i-frames, compared to most other classes having 8 or 9 i-frames) and needs 3 points in Adaptability or 9 points in Attunement to improve this to 8 i-frames.

title: Bandit (Dark Souls II)
snippet:
Bandits are actually unable to speak to Straid of Olaphis by default, the only class that can't do that, due to its extremely low Intelligence not meeting his minimum required amount of 3.

The starting weapons are somewhat mixed, with the Short Bow following the higher starting value in Dexterity while the Hand Axe instead focuses on Strength. The Hand Axe is most likely better replaced with an actually Dexterity-focused weapon, though those are in limited supply until Blacksmith Lenigrast's shop is opened, mostly the Dagger in Things Betwixt and the Halberd in the Forest of Fallen Giants. Beyond extra weapons such as the Spear and the Rapier, Lenigrast also holds the game's first infinite supply of ammunition (merely more Wood Arrows, but still) and another Short Bow.

title: Cleric (Dark Souls II)
snippet:
Cleric (Dark Souls II) -  Dark Souls II - mechanic - lead 
 lead : The **Cleric** is one of the classes in *Dark Souls 2*.

The Cleric is a Faith-based starting class with decent Vigor, Attunement, and Strength, making it a good base for any Faith-focused build, such as a pure Miracles and Lightning build, or a more mixed Hexes build that wants to start with some extra healing spells. It is also a decent base for a more paladin-style build that wants to use heavy weapons but that also wants some extra healing in the beginning.

title: Cleric (Dark Souls II)
snippet: While this class may seem to have below average defences with only decent Poise, since all of those stats come from one piece of equipment, the Archdrake Robes, those defences can be improved greatly by adding more armor, even if that is just putting back on some pieces from the Imported Set from before the character creation. If up to buying armor pieces, the Falconer Set head, hands, and legs pieces provide a good mix of defences and Poise at a relatively low price of roughly 1,000 souls per piece. Be wary that that this will shorten the character's roll distance unless Vitality is increased, with all the extra Imported Set pieces (head, hands, and legs) increasing defence by about 45% but giving no extra poise and shortening rolls by 10%, wearing the Falconer Helm and Boots increases defence by 85% and poise by 100% at the cost of 2,100 souls and shortening rolls by 10%, and wearing the Falconer Helm, Gloves, and Boots increases defence by 110% and poise by 130% at the cost of

title: Cleric (Dark Souls II)
snippet:
The Heal Miracle equipped by default is quite strong early on. While it isn't as strong as the Soul Arrow of the Sorcerer it can heavily supplement the very few starting charges of the Estus Flask, even more so if a second copy is bought of off Merchant Hag Melentia.

Despite its decent Attunement and having an 8 i-frame roll, its low Adaptability means it is pretty far down in the Agility department and needs either 3 points in Adaptability or 9 points in Attunement to improve to 9 i-frames.

title: Cleric (Dark Souls II)
snippet: Their Mace is actually a pretty strong weapon as its Strike damage is highly valuable and as a Hammer it has an above average Counter Strength of 120, meaning it deals extra damage on Counter Attacks. However, it does have one slight disadvantage in that it has a Strength requirement of 12 while the Cleric only starts with 11 Strength and thus needs 1 more point in the stat to deal the weapon one-handed instead of only two-handed. The Cleric's Sacred Chime is decent for the offensive, Lightning-based Miracles but is mediocre for chime-based Hexes due to its lower Dark-scaling. However, it does have good casting speed so it is a good alternative for support Miracles since it can be left unupgraded so that all the character's titanite can be used on their other equipment.

title: Deprived (Dark Souls II)
snippet:
Deprived (Dark Souls II) -  Dark Souls II - mechanic - lead 
 lead : The **Deprived** is one of the classes in *Dark Souls 2*.

Unlike the other classes, it doesn't start with any weapons or Lifegems and only has the unequipped Imported Set as armor. Make sure to retrieve the Dagger found in the first side path of Things Betwixt as an initial weapon, while the Morning Star in Majula can be wielded two-handed with 2 more Strength and 1 more Dexterity. A Cleric's Sacred Chime can be found near the Morning Star if wanting to use Miracles, a Shield can be gained by either buying one of Maughlin the Armorer in Majula or be found on the path to Heide's Tower of Flame, and a Sorcerer's Staff can be found behind a hidden wall in the Forest of Fallen Giants.

The low level means leveling up is slightly cheaper than for any other class, and the all-6 statline serves as a decent base for a build focused on the Mundane infusion since that scales of the lowest stat.

title: Deprived (Dark Souls II)
snippet: Its average Adaptability and Attunment means it actually starts with a decent, 8 i-frame roll.

title: Explorer
snippet:
For restocking the items, Merchant Hag Melentia carries more Lifegems and Witching Urns and 1 more Pharros' Lockstone, Laddersmith Gilligan has Aromatic Oozes, Wood Bolts are sold by Blacksmith Lenigrast, Repair Powders are sold in limited quantities by Blacksmiths and infinitely by one late-game merchant, Prism Stones are sold by Sweet Shalquoir, and 5 more Rusted Coins are sold by Magerold of Lanafir.

Their high Adaptability gives them 9 i-frames when starting out, and they only need 2 more points in the stat to improve that to 10 i-frames.

title: Explorer
snippet:
The Traveling Merchant Set is only a bit better than the Imported Set and has no Poise but the hat increases Item Discovery slightly, which is a solid benefit early on.

The lone Pharros' Lockstone can be used to unlock 1 (and only one, since it is a consumable) Pharros' Contraption. Of the first two Contraptions to be found in the game, the first one is below a trapped room with ballistae in the Forest of Fallen Giants and used to get the Chloranthy Ring and a Titanite Slab, and the second one is found one a small platform up halfway up the first set of stairs in No-man's Wharf where it is used turn on the lights and scare away all the Dark Stalkers in the area.

title: Explorer
snippet:
Explorer -  Dark Souls II - mechanic - lead 
 lead : The **Explorer** is one of the classes in *Dark Souls 2*.

It has no particular specialty, with only high Adaptability and an above average Vitality being notable. It is, essentially, a Deprived with some extra stats, some bonus items, and a Dagger.

As their Dagger is the only weapon they start out with, with not even a spell to help them, it is imperative to pick up a second Dagger in Things Betwixt on the first side path fore more Durability. Is is possible to wield the Morning Star from the cliffs in Majula two-handed with 2 more points in Strength and one more point in Dexterity, and a Light Crossbow can be found atop a wall in the Forest of Fallen Giants and only need 1 more point in Strength to wield with two hands.

The Traveling Merchant Set is only a bit better than the Imported Set and has no Poise but the hat increases Item Discovery slightly, which is a solid benefit early on.

title: Knight (Dark Souls II)
snippet:
While its Broadsword is a good starting weapon its lack of a shield should probably be rectified quickly by buying either the Silver Eagle Kite Shield or, with some improvements to Strength, the Twin Dragon Greatshield from Maughlin so that rolling isn't the only defence.

The Knight class's high Adaptability gives it enough Agility that it only needs 1 more point in either Attunement or Adaptability to improves its roll from 8 i-frames to 9 i-frames, which is a great boon.

title: Knight (Dark Souls II)
snippet:
Knight (Dark Souls II) -  Dark Souls II - mechanic - lead 
 lead : The **Knight** is one of the classes in *Dark Souls 2*.

This class's high starting Vigor, in combination with its decent Adaptability, makes it a good bit more sturdy than most of the other classes. On the offensive side it has a decent starting Strength and slightly above average Faith, lending it well towards Strength- or Lightning-based weapons, though any aspirations towards spells (and especially Sorceries) are somewhat hampered by its rather low Attunement and Intelligence

The Falconer Set pieces it is wearing have good physical defence and has the highest Poise of all starting set, even with it missing the helmet (which can be bought from Maughlin the Armorer in Majula), making it more resistant to being staggered than other classes at the start.

title: Sorcerer (Dark Souls II)
snippet:
The initial Soul Arrow spell is fairly strong, strong enough to be able to kill any of the first few Ogres in the game, whether that be the Stone Ring-holding one before the hut in Things Betwixt or the Scholar of the First Sin-exclusive one on the path to the Forest of Fallen Giants, giving a fair amount of early souls. Make sure to pick up a second copy from Merchant Hag Melentia to double the amount of uses.

The head and hands pieces of the Imported Set can be put on for an extra 40% defence, at the cost of shortening the distance of their rolls by about 10% unless Vitality is increased.

The combination of above average Adaptability and high Attunement gives the class one of the best starting rolls, at 9 i-frames.

title: Sorcerer (Dark Souls II)
snippet:
Sorcerer (Dark Souls II) -  Dark Souls II - mechanic - lead 
 lead : The **Sorcerer** is one of the classes in *Dark Souls 2*.

It is an Intelligence-based class, serving as an excellent base for a build focused on Sorceries or Hexes, and also possibly for a build using a Magic infused weapon that wants to start with some spells. It has a decent starting Dexterity but a horrendous starting Strength, barely even enough to wield their weapon and even with effective Strength being doubled when two-handing so the vast majority of weapons can't be wielded without some investment, only some Daggers.

The starting Sorcerer's Staff is a decent, quick-casting spell tool for Sorceries that is worth upgrading, while the Dagger is a decent, if short reaching weapon whose poor Durability should be supplemented by picking up a second copy in the Things Betwixt tutorial.

title: Swordsman
snippet:
Swordsman -  Dark Souls II - mechanic - lead 
 lead : The **Swordsman** is one of the classes in *Dark Souls 2*.

It has the highest Dexterity of the starting classes, making it a good base for a build focused on that stat, such as one using Curved Swords and Bows. Additionally, a decent base Attunement and Intelligence makes using support Sorceries such as Magic Weapon easier.

The starting weapons this class wields are the only ones that are upgraded (though only to +1) and are compatible with each other for the purpose of Power Stancing, though another 2 points in Strength and 8 points in Dexterity are needed for that. Instead, it may be easier to either focus on one of the weapons as the main weapon, with perhaps a shield from Maughlin the Armorer in the other hand, or to get a second Shortsword from the Forest of Fallen Giants as that only requires the 2 extra points in Strength to begin Power Stancing.

title: Swordsman
snippet:
The initial armor set, the Wanderer Set, has overall decent defences and is quite light but has no poise, making it nearly useless if trying to directly exchange blows.

At 8 i-frames it has a decent starting roll, but due to having the lowest starting HP (only about 740 hp, with only the Sorcerer and Deprived having similarly low hp at about 770 each while the other classes range from 830 hp to 960 hp) because of its low Vigor, getting that stat and then Adaptability up a bit will be good for actually surviving the hits that land. Its low Vitality makes the class somewhat limited in what it can carry while still keeping a decent roll.

This can easiest be done by picking up the Morning Star found by dropping through the hole in the rocks to the left of the wooden fence seen just after exiting Things Betwixt, or by taking the dagger found inside the first sidepath fog gate of Things Betwixt.

title: Warrior (Dark Souls II)
snippet:
Warrior (Dark Souls II) -  Dark Souls II - mechanic - lead 
 lead : The **Warrior** is one of the classes in *Dark Souls 2*.

They have the highest starting Strength and have notably above average Dexterity, lending it well towards builds that want to either focus on Strength-based weapons with a moderate Dexterity requirement or to use weapons that scale well with both of those stats. This is also the only class in Dark Souls 2 to start out with a shield, the Iron Parma. While this shield can also be bought by other classes from Maughlin the Armorer, available from the start of the game, and is largely outclassed by the Silver Eagle Kite Shield that can also be bought from him, it's still a nice tool to have early on with its decent Physical blocking and Stability, and to save on souls early on before replacing it.

title: Assassin (class)
snippet:
The Assassin Set has only moderate physical defences but has good magic and fire defences, and high overall resistances against anything that isn't Bleed.

While the **Assassin** doesn't have any ranged attack, its Spook Sorcery is extremely useful for removing most non-fatal fall damage and for completely silencing footsteps for 20 seconds, allowing certain obstacles to be bypassed . Unfortunately, while the starting Sorcerer's Staff is a fairly good spell tool, if not exactly the best, it won't actually start to gain scaling from stats until Intelligence has reached at least 19, delaying a possible strengthening of the character's Sorceries.

Picking up the Soul Arrow Sorcery from the Shrine Handmaid gives a reusable ranged attack early on, while the weapon buffing Magic Weapon Sorcery can be gained in either Undead Settlement or Road of Sacrifices to add some of a Staff's spellbuff to weapon damage.

title: Assassin (class)
snippet:
Assassin (class) -  Dark Souls III - mechanic - lead 
 lead : The **Assassin** is one of the classes in *Dark Souls 3*.

It is a Dexterity-based class with decent Attunement for Weapon Arts and spells and some Intelligence for Sorceries.

An unusually long Thrusting Sword, the Estoc is also quite strong and has a rare sweeping heavy attack for hitting several or agile foes easier, at the cost of not having an increased critical modifier for Ripostes and Backstabs. Additionally, its Weapon Art, Shield Splitter, helps with its bad damage to the stamina of blocking targets by partially bypassing the defences of the block instead.

Its Targeting Shield, while not very suitable for blocking, is one of the game's three parrying shields and as such its Parry starts slightly earlier yet ends as late as the regular parry.

The Assassin Set has only moderate physical defences but has good magic and fire defences, and high overall resistances against anything that isn't Bleed.

title: Assassin (class)
snippet:
Assassin (class) -  Dark Souls III - mechanic - trivia 
 trivia : This class is fairly popular amongst speedrunners thanks to Spook making it possible to easier skip foes and falls.
While the Assassin doesn't have any direct equivalent class in the Dark Souls series, it does bear some resemblance to the Royalty class from FromSoftware's previous game Demon's Souls, another Dexterity/Intelligence-based class wielding a thrusting sword (in that case a Rapier) and a small shield while also providing access to a Sorcery-like spell (though in the Royalty's case it is the offensive Soul Arrow, not a self-buffing spell).

title: Attunement (Dark Souls II)
snippet:
Attunement (Dark Souls II) -  Dark Souls II - mechanic - general_information 
 general_information : Attunement determines the number of spell slots the player has available to equip spells, and also increases the player's Cast Speed (this effect is roughly double that of leveling Intelligence or Faith). In addition to these, raising Attunement also increases the number of casts per slot a spell has; however, this varies from spell to spell. Raising Attunement also increases the player's Curse Resist and Agility slightly, and as with every other stat, HP is increased by minute amounts each time.

**20/25/30** are the softcaps for attunement that you’d generally want to stop at for a caster build in terms of spell slots. The caps for attunement are **30/75** for spell slots, **94** for max number of spell casts, and around **50-55** for spell casting speed in conjunction with 50 Faith or Intelligence.

title: Attunement (Dark Souls II)
snippet:
Attunement (Dark Souls II) -  Dark Souls II - mechanic - notes 
 notes : Players that want to make the most out of Attunement without investing fully in it should note that most spells that have very little uses, will be almost maxed out at 49. Most spells that have a maximum of 3 uses will be at 2, those that have a maximum of 4 will be at 3, and the same math applies to all those that have 5 and 6 maximum uses. This is important to take into consideration should players want to make Faith or Pyromancy builds, as most spells of those categories are often of very low uses.

title: Attunement (Dark Souls III)
snippet:
Attunement (Dark Souls III) -  Dark Souls III - mechanic - lead 
 lead : **Attunement** is a stat in *Dark Souls III* that increases the player character's Focus Points, or FP as well as increasing the number of Attunement slots.

Focus Points are used to cast Sorceries, Pyromancies and Miracles, as well as performing skills.

Spells can be attuned at the bonfire, provided the player has available Attunement slots. A minimum investment of 10 Attunement is required for one Attunement slot.

As it is with every other stat in the game, it also has indirect bonuses such as increasing the player character's flat defenses.

Leveling Attunement provides the following benefits:

Diminishing returns for increasing the amount of FP begin at 35 Attunement, while every 10 Attunement past 30 (except at 80 Attunement) will grant an additional slot. Equipping any one of the Saint's Ring, Deep Ring and Darkmoon Ring will grant 1, 1 and 2 additional Attunement slots, respectively.

title: Attunement (Dark Souls III)
snippet: At 99 Attunement, the player will have 450 FP and 10 Attunement slots.

snippet:
Attunement (Dark Souls) -  Dark Souls - mechanic - notes 
 notes : The maximum possible amount of slots is 12 when Attunement is 50 when Darkmoon Seance Ring and White Seance Ring are both slotted.
Attuning multiple copies of the same sorcery, miracle or pyromancy will stack the number of uses; however, this will not change how many uses one gets per slot.
Most spells require only one Attunement slot. Some, however, require two. All Chaos pyromancies, Sunlight Spear, Bountiful Sunlight, Soothing Sunlight and Pursuers are examples of this.

title: Attunement (Dark Souls)
snippet:
Attunement (Dark Souls) -  Dark Souls - mechanic - general_information 
 general_information : This stat governs how many Attunement slots the player has, which in turn allows players to equip and use more types of magic at once. It is also possible to increase Attunement slots through equipping Darkmoon Seance Ring and White Seance Ring.

Softcaps for Attunement are **16/19/23** with 50 being the hardcap for spell slots. Leveling Attunement beyond 50 gives no benefits aside from a couple points in various defenses. For a caster build it is not advisable to level Attunement beyond 23.

title: Casting Speed
snippet:
Casting Speed -  Dark Souls II - mechanic - notes 
 notes : Casting speed is influenced by Attunement, Faith, and Intelligence.
One level of Attunement will increase cast speed at twice the rate of one level of Faith or Intelligence.
Menu Casting speed rises by two points until it is 115, actual casting speed is entirely linear in its levels.

title: Casting Speed
snippet:
Casting Speed -  Dark Souls II - mechanic - mechanics 
 mechanics : Despite what the menu says, Casting Speed is simply a percentage that multiplies how long the startup of a spell will last. The menu numbers are only usable in so far as telling you what stats can affect natural casting speed.

The menu implies a softcap for casting speed from leveling while it actuality it doesn't exist.

Your natural Casting Speed level is determined by your Attunement, Intelligence and Faith levels, with the formula:

Each Spell has a defined startup duration, which is the part that can be affected by casting speed. Every Spell Casting Tool has a value that multiplies your natural casting speed. Every piece of Casting Gear has a value that multiplies your natural casting.

Your total casting speed is the product of multiplying your natural Casting Speed with each piece of casting gear being used and the Spell Casting Tool that is being used.

title: Casting Speed
snippet:
Casting Speed -  Dark Souls II - mechanic - lead 
 lead : **Casting speed** is a stat in *Dark Souls II*.

A character's casting speed decides how quickly they can cast spells. It affects the entire startup animation. In the adjoined video you can count frames and see the animations only differentiate before bringing the chime up to the character's left side.

Casting speed affects all types of magic, and appears to get diminishing returns on quick casting magic. This means that spells like Soul Arrow and Resonant Soul will get only a marginal boost after a certain level of casting speed, while slower magic like Lightning Spear and Chaos Storm will cast considerably faster with higher casting speed.

All catalysts also have their own casting speeds. This speed affects the speed of the cast equally to the player's stat. Examples of catalysts with high casting speed are Caitha's Chime and the Dragon Chime. It is also possible to increase casting speed by wearing a Clear Bluestone Ring.

title: Cleric
snippet:
At an initial level of 2, Clerics have the second-lowest starting level (the lowest being Pyromancers) of any class. They start the game as a member of the Way of White covenant.

Joining the Warriors of Sunlight can allow Clerics to become powerful magical attackers early on in the game, giving them the miracle Lightning Spear. Astora's Straight Sword and Dragon Crest Shield are also very useful early game pick-ups for the Cleric, provided they choose the Master Key as their gift and enter Valley of Drakes via New Londo Ruins. The former scales with Faith, allowing the Cleric to focus exclusively on it, while the latter is a far better shield than that which the Cleric starts with.

title: Cleric
snippet:
Cleric -  Dark Souls - mechanic - lead 
 lead : The **Cleric** is one of the classes in *Dark Souls*.

Clerics can use miracles to heal, due to their high starting Faith stat and equipped Talisman. They also start with a strong melee weapon in the form of the Mace, but little in the way of defense. Clerics are well suited to heavier weapon types, such as Hammers, as taking on enemies directly with slower weapons is offset by their ability to heal more often than other classes.

At an initial level of 2, Clerics have the second-lowest starting level (the lowest being Pyromancers) of any class. They start the game as a member of the Way of White covenant.

title: Cleric (Dark Souls III)
snippet:
Cleric (Dark Souls III) -  Dark Souls III - mechanic - lead 
 lead : The **Cleric** is one of the classes in *Dark Souls 3*.

It is a Faith-focused class, with decent Attunement, Strength, and Luck. This makes them well-suited to a Miracle-heavy build, and to using the many Lightning-attuned weapons as they are often also have good Strength-scaling.

While it does indeed have spells, in the form of Heal (which heals) and Force (which throws enemies away from you), it does not have any that causes damage, with the earliest ones not being found until Cathedral of the Deep or Farron Keep. This means the class will have to focus primarily on weapons initially, and will do well to keep them upgraded as offensive Miracles consume a lot of Focus Points.

title: Cleric (Dark Souls III)
snippet:
Cleric (Dark Souls III) -  Dark Souls III - mechanic - trivia 
 trivia : This is the only spellcasting-focused starting class in Dark Souls 3 that doesn't have a damage-boosting ring. Presumably this is because the Cleric doesn't have a damaging Miracle equipped from the start, and the Morne's Ring can instead be found in the Road of Sacrifices.
This class has remained remarkably similar throughout the series, always carrying a Mace and the Heal Miracle.

title: Cleric (Dark Souls III)
snippet: The Cleric's Sacred Chime is a fairly good casting tool and is actually the strongest casting tool for Miracles from 45 to 49 Faith. Its Spell Buff (the stat that affects how strong scaling spells are) doesn't actually increase until at least 19 Faith has been reached. Its Weapon Art is Gentle Prayer, a regenerative effect that always restores 360 hp over the course of a minute as long as the Chime is held in an active hand (so replacing it with another item stops it, as does two-handing the item in the other hand). This effect will actually outheal the Heal Miracle by up to 20% until the Chime's Spell Buff reaches 120, and even afterwards it is a strong if slow alternative due to only having about a third the cost in Focus Points.

title: Cleric (Dark Souls III)
snippet:
The Cleric Set is a light, caster-type armor set and as such has low physical defences and high elemental defences, while also having high Poison and Curse resistances.

The first trainer for more Miracles is found in the Undead Settlement for further development.

title: Cleric (Dark Souls III)
snippet:
The Mace is an unexpectedly strong weapon for what may at first seem like a spellcasting class, but in reality it is often a **Cleric's** main armament. This is because Strike damage is often the strongest physical damage type as armored and skeletal enemies are weak to it (most other physical damage types have fewer enemies weak to them), strong Strength-scaling for easy damage increases, a fairly good moveset, and has a good Weapon Art for trading hits with opponents. How the Weapon Art works is that Perseverance adds a flat 45% extra absorption and causes the attacks of light weapons to bounce off the user, while also granting great Hyper Armor to prevent being staggered.

The Blue Wooden Shield is not very good, having only decent physical and magic defence with serviceable Stability. While it does have Parry (albeit the inferior Medium Shield version), a strong Weapon Skill shield like the early Silver Eagle Kite Shield would probably serve as a better replacement.

title: Curved Greatswords (Dark Souls II)
snippet:
Curved Greatswords (Dark Souls II) -  Dark Souls II - weapon - lead 
 lead : **Curved Greatswords** are a type of weapon in *Dark Souls II*.

Handled as a blend between greatswords and ultra greatswords, the Curved Greatsword class are weapons that excel at damage output with speeds comparable to that of smaller weapons. Boasting relatively fast one-handed, horizontal swings, and vertical, two-handed swings, which can vary in speeds when used as a follow-up attack. They require moderate amounts of stat investment to use; making them slightly less accessible. As a result of having ultra greatsword-like properties, they have similar riposte and backstab damage.

Endurance (Dark Souls II) -  Dark Souls II - mechanic - general_information 
 general_information : Increasing one's Endurance affects several attributes of the player. Endurance's main effect is to increase both the player's Stamina, as well as their total HP however, this does not increase it as much as raising Vigor will. Endurance is also interactive with Strength, Dexterity and Vitality, the sum of which determines the player's natural Physical Defense. Finally, Endurance is also interactive with the Adaptability stat, in that raising the two stats at the same rate will grant extra natural Poise.

Unlike in *Dark Souls* and *Demon's Souls*, raising Endurance does not improve a character's Equip Load.

snippet:
Backstep -  Dark Souls - mechanic - lead 
 lead : Backstepping is a gameplay mechanic in Dark Souls.

A backstep is performed by pressing the roll key without pressing in any direction. The player will then take a leap backwards instead of rolling.

Backstepping also grants invincibility frames, but fewer than rolling. While rolling gives 11 i-frames, backsteps only give 4. Equipping the Dark Wood Grain Ring replaces the backstep with a backwards ninja flip with 8 i-frames. This may now seem like backstepping is generally worse that rolling. However, backstepping has two situational advantages over rolling.

title: Daggers (Dark Souls III)
snippet:
Daggers (Dark Souls III) -  Dark Souls III - weapon - lead 
 lead : **Daggers** are a type of weapon in *Dark Souls III*. Daggers are characterized by their fast attack speed and high critical damage. Daggers are one of the smallest weapon types. Careful tactical consideration should be taken by the player while using these weapons as you need to be very close to successfully attack. Basic "hit and run" strategy and critical attacks are a hallmark of this weapon type. Most daggers receive the Quickstep weapon skill, granting them increased movement even in normally bogged areas such as swamps and deep water. In addition to quicker movement, the quickstep skill grants the player increased invincibility frames. This skill can be enhanced by the Carthus Bloodring, granting even more invincibility frames.

title: Rolling
snippet:
Rolling -  Dark Souls - mechanic - medium_roll_mid_roll 
 medium_roll_mid_roll : Players have Mid Roll if their equipment weight is 26% to 50% of their maximum equipment load. Just like the fast roll, there are several different categories that affect speed of recovery after the roll: Medium rolls have 14 instability frames in their animation meaning there are more frames where the player takes 1.4x additional damage than they have iframes. This means that if the player is at Mid Roll weight, they should lean into Poise and Defense mechanics rather than rolling. The 1.4x additional damage taken during Instability Frames is enough to partially or fully negate the defenses that player armor provides. While at Mid Roll weight player speed during actions like sprinting and walking will be reduced slightly.

title: Poison (Dark Souls II)
snippet:
Poison (Dark Souls II) -  Dark Souls II - mechanic - poison_attack_bonus 
 poison_attack_bonus : The Poison Attack Bonus (abbreviated as Poison BNS in-game) increases the amount of Poison buildup inflicted per hit. It does not affect the total amount of damage the poison will do. Unlike weapons that have a magical scaling stat, Poison has no equivalent scaling.

The Poison BNS value is determined by the Dexterity and Adaptability stats. In order to continually increase innate Poison BNS, both Dexterity and Adaptability need to be leveled up, with Dexterity giving a larger bonus.

title: Vitality (Dark Souls)
snippet:
Vitality (Dark Souls) -  Dark Souls - mechanic - lead 
 lead : **Vitality** is one of the eight base stats in *Dark Souls* that can be increased when leveling up. Investing in vitality increases the player's maximum health points (HP).

Contrary to the vitality stats in *Dark Souls II* and *Dark Souls III*, vitality in *Dark Souls* does not affect the player's maximum equipment load. In *Dark Souls*, equipment load is governed by endurance.

title: Rolling
snippet:
Rolling -  Dark Souls - mechanic - general_information 
 general_information : Contrary to popular belief, all roll types have 11 iframes except for the roll type associated with Dark Wood Grain Ring (also called Ninja Flip) which has 13 iframes. The main differences between roll types is the overall length of the animation coupled with Recovery Frames and Instability Frames. Instability Frames are the most critical aspect of rolling, as these are points in the animation where the player character will take 1.4x additional damage when hit. Dark Wood Grain Ring roll type is the only roll with no Instability Frames.

title: Negative Status Effects (Dark Souls II)
snippet:
Negative Status Effects (Dark Souls II) -  Dark Souls II - mechanic - waterlogged 
 waterlogged : The waterlogged status increases fire defense by 300 but reduces lightning defense by 150. The duration of the status depends on how much the water covered the player, with rolling applying the maximum duration. Additionally, it can affect both players and enemies, with bosses like Looking Glass Knight and Demon of Song being permanently waterlogged due to their arenas.

Additionally, being covered in water will wash off poison and oil.

title: Force
snippet:
Force -  Dark Souls - spell - counters 
 counters : Rolling at the right time against a Force user negates all staggering effect Force has. Staying away from cliff faces will minimize the chances of being blasted off. Force is much more dangerous in confined areas, so try to fight in open spaces against a Force user.

In terms of equipment, wearing very light equipment allows players to be knocked off their feet, granting invincibility frames; on the other end of the spectrum, using a shield with high stability will minimize the potential danger Force users pose.
